## Claims

### C-R2-001
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo treats 1:19–20 as a brief, traditionally Jewish wisdom exhortation on improper speech and anger, transitional introduction to the major unit 1:21–2:26 rather than an outline unit equal to 2:18 or 1:21–2:26; “my dear brothers” signals topic switch, and “therefore” in v. 21 makes 19–20 basis for accepting the word.
- **quote:** "it is better to view them as a transitional introduction to the major unit that follows. The address \"my dear brothers\" usually introduces a new topic in the letter of James… And the \"therefore\" of v. 21 shows that the negative warnings of vv. 19-20 act as the basis for the positive exhortation to \"accept the word.\""
- **locus:** L5
- **passage:** James 1:19–20 intro

### C-R2-002
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo prefers reading Greek *iste* as imperative (“take note of this,” NIV) rather than indicative (“this you know,” NASB); rejects KJV “wherefore” as based on a variant that should not be accepted.
- **quote:** "the imperative is more likely here since this is the kind of verb that James usually pairs with his address \"my beloved brothers.\" This general call to pay attention signals a pause in James's argument as he switches from one topic to another."
- **locus:** L7
- **passage:** James 1:19

### C-R2-003
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo rejects the popular view that the object of “be quick to listen / slow to speak” is the word of God (v. 18; 21–25): that would force “slow to speak” the word into a 3:1-like teacher warning (hard without 3:1) and leave the parallel “slow to anger” unexplained.
- **quote:** "If this were so, the command to be \"slow to speak\" the word of God would have to have a sense similar to Jas. 3:1… But this idea would be difficult to discover without 3:1… Moreover, the third, grammatically parallel command, \"be slow to anger,\" is difficult to explain on this reading of the verse."
- **locus:** L9
- **passage:** James 1:19

### C-R2-004
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo grounds 1:19 in widespread Jewish wisdom on listening much and talking little (Prov. 17:28; 10:19; 11:12–13; 13:3; Sir. 5:11–13) and the link of hasty speech with unrighteous anger (Prov. 17:27): uncontrolled anger leads to uncontrolled speech; the wise control anger to curb hasty speech.
- **quote:** "an even better reason for rejecting the \"word of God\" interpretation is James's obvious dependence on a widespread Jewish wisdom teaching about speech and anger… Uncontrolled anger leads to uncontrolled speech… The wise person, James reminds us, will therefore learn to control the emotion of anger and so eliminate one of the most common sources of hasty and unwise speech."
- **locus:** L11
- **passage:** James 1:19

### C-R2-005
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Against psychologists who claim emotions can only be suppressed or ignored, Moo says James (and similar biblical exhortations) presume emotions can be transformed by God’s grace and the Spirit so as to align with God’s word and will.
- **quote:** "Psychologists will sometimes claim that emotions, since they are a natural product of the personality, cannot truly be controlled - only suppressed or ignored. But James's exhortation here (and many similar biblical exhortations) presume differently. Emotions are the product of the entire person; and, by God's grace and the work of the Spirit, the person can be transformed so as to bring emotions in line with God's word and will."
- **locus:** L11
- **passage:** James 1:19

### C-R2-006
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo argues that “the righteousness of God” (lit.; NIV “righteous life that God desires”) in 1:20 must not be read through Paul’s gospel use (Rom. 1:17; 3:21–22): James writes before Paul and should be read against OT, Judaism, and Jesus; “do/produce righteousness” means do what God requires of his people (cf. Matt. 5:20), not God’s act/gift of righteousness or rare “exact justice.”
- **quote:** "perhaps no greater mistake can be made in interpreting James than to read his letter in the light of Paul… James must be read against the background of the OT, Judaism, and the teaching of Jesus - not the apostle Paul… We are on firmer ground in thinking that James uses the phrase \"produce righteousness\" with the meaning it normally has in the Bible: do what God requires of his people… James's very simple point is that human anger does not produce behavior that is pleasing to God."
- **locus:** L13–L15
- **passage:** James 1:20

### C-R2-007
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo does not take 1:19–20 as prohibiting all anger including “righteous anger”: as wisdom genre, apparently absolute assertions make general proverbial points; human anger is usually not pleasing to God, leading to sins (violence, murder, unwise speech).
- **quote:** "Does James intend to prohibit all anger of any kind - even what we sometimes called \"righteous anger\"? Probably not. James falls into the wisdom genre at this point. And wisdom sayings are notorious for the use of apparently absolute assertions in order to make a general, \"proverbial\" point… human anger is not usually pleasing to God, leading as it does to all kinds of sins."
- **locus:** L17
- **passage:** James 1:20

### C-R2-008
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo states the theme of 1:21–27: those born by God’s word (v. 18) must “accept” that word (v. 21) by doing it (vv. 22–27); practical obedience is signaled by shift from “word” to “law” (v. 25) and frequency of “doer”; religion that counts and can save must express itself in obedience to the implanted word.
- **quote:** "The theme of this paragraph is obvious: those who have experienced the new birth by means of God's word (v. 18) must \"accept\" that word (v. 21) by doing it (vv. 22-27)… The \"religion\" that counts before God (v. 27) and that is able to save the soul (v. 21) must come to expression in a lifestyle of obedience to the word of God, \"implanted\" within each believer (v. 21)."
- **locus:** L23
- **passage:** James 1:21–27 intro

### C-R2-009
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo places the main transition at v. 21 (not between 21 and 22): “therefore” may connect 21–27 with v. 18 more than with 19–20; similar new-birth → “get rid of” evil → embrace the word sequence appears independently in 1 Pet. 1:23–2:2, suggesting shared early-church teaching.
- **quote:** "Most English translations and commentators put the transition between vv. 21 and 22. But the introduction of the topic of the \"word\" in v. 21 suggests that it belongs with the material following it. The therefore at the beginning of v. 21… may connect the discussion in vv. 21-27 with v. 18 rather than with vv. 19-20. And a close connection between v. 18 and vv. 21-27 is suggested by a similar sequence of ideas in 1 Pet. 1:23-2:2."
- **locus:** L25
- **passage:** James 1:21 structure

### C-R2-010
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo explains *apotithemai* (“get rid of” / “take off”) as clothing imagery applied metaphorically to stripping pre-Christian lifestyle (Rom. 13:12; Eph. 4:22, 25; Col. 3:8; Heb. 12:1; 1 Pet. 2:1)—another sign James cites common early Christian teaching; participle is virtually imperative.
- **quote:** "The NIV rid yourselves of translates a Gk. verb (apotithemai) that means to \"take off.\" The word connotes the idea of removing clothes… and the imagery is applied metaphorically in the NT to the \"stripping off\" of the pre-Christian lifestyle from the believer… James's use of this term is another indication that he is probably citing common early Christian teaching here."
- **locus:** L27
- **passage:** James 1:21

### C-R2-011
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo takes “moral filth” (*rhyparia*, only here in the Bible; adj. in 2:2 for poor man’s clothes; Zech. 3:3–4 garments) as ethical “filth/sordidness” underscoring how offensive sin is; “evil that is so prevalent” means abundance/surplus of evil (*perisseia*, not “remainder”), so putting off sin is a fight against a many-formed foe.
- **quote:** "James chooses a word that reminds us just how offensive and detestable sin really is… The Greek word involved (perisseia) is used three other times in the NT… each time with the meaning \"abundance.\" James warns believers that putting off sin involves a fight against a foe that takes many different forms."
- **locus:** L29
- **passage:** James 1:21

### C-R2-012
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo rejects reading *emphytos* as “inborn” natural capacity to apprehend revelation: “the word” saves (v. 21), regenerates (v. 18), and equates with the law of liberty (v. 25)—so it is the gospel word implanted in believers, drawn especially from Jeremiah 31:33 (new covenant law written on hearts; cf. Ezek. 36:24–32).
- **quote:** "James must be referring to the word of the gospel and not to an innate quality within human beings… If this is James's meaning, then emphytos will have the sense \"implanted\" rather than \"innate.\"… James likely draws this striking conception of the implanted word from the famous new covenant prophecy of Jeremiah 31… God promises to put his law within his people, to write it on their hearts (Jer. 31:33)."
- **locus:** L31–L33
- **passage:** James 1:21

### C-R2-013
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** For Moo, “humbly accept the word planted in you” is not an evangelistic call to conversion but a command to believers to let the implanted word influence all of life; “save your souls” portrays salvation as future deliverance at Christ’s return (cf. 2:14; 4:12; 5:20), important for James’s theology.
- **quote:** "the command to accept the word implanted in you is not a command to unbelievers to be converted… but to believers to allow the word to influence them in all parts of their lives… We should especially note that James here portrays salvation as future from the standpoint of the believer… This perspective on salvation is important to keep in mind if we are to understand James's theology correctly."
- **locus:** L35
- **passage:** James 1:21

### C-R2-014
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo holds that “accept” the word (v. 21) is the main point of 21–27, specified in 22–25 as “do” it; v. 22 is “rightly the best-known verse in the letter”; James does not diminish hearing but opposes *mere* hearing; implanted-word imagery does not license passivity or automatic knowledge of God’s will.
- **quote:** "James's exhortation to Christians to \"accept\" the implanted word (v. 21) is the main point of vv. 21-27… Essentially, James argues in vv. 22-25, to \"accept\" the word means to \"do\" it… And so it is… with this exhortation we find ourselves right at the heart of James's pastoral concern; and v. 22 is rightly the best-known verse in the letter… It is not listening to the word that James opposes or diminishes, but merely listening."
- **locus:** L37
- **passage:** James 1:22

### C-R2-015
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo situates hearer/doer concern in wider Greco-Roman “practice what you preach,” Jewish “not the expounding but the doing,” Paul’s Rom. 2:13, and especially Jesus (Luke 11:28): both gracious divine initiative and grateful human obedience are necessary aspects of the gospel.
- **quote:** "Both the gracious initiative of God and the grateful response of human beings are necessary aspects of the gospel. The word, through which we are born into new life (v. 18) and which becomes implanted in us (v. 21), is a word that must be put into practice."
- **locus:** L39
- **passage:** James 1:22

### C-R2-016
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: mere listeners “deceive themselves” (same verb as Col. 2:4)—blinded to true religious state; even regular hearers who do not do are not truly right with God; failure to do anticipates 2:14–26 and suggests they have not truly accepted God’s word.
- **quote:** "to be \"deceived\" is to be blinded to the reality of one's true religious state… And so it is for those people who \"hear\" the word… but do not \"do\" it. They are mistaken in thinking that they are truly right with God… The person who fails to do the word, James therefore suggests (in an anticipation of his argument in 2:14-26), is a person who has not truly accepted God's word at all."
- **locus:** L41
- **passage:** James 1:22

### C-R2-017
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** On the mirror simile, Moo prefers *genesis* with “face” as “existence” in a relatively neutral sense—“natural face” (what one actually sees)—not “face of origin” as ideal creational image, and not heavy negative “sinful existence”; v. 24’s simple “himself” confirms not over-reading the phrase.
- **quote:** "The second meaning of the word, \"existence,\" is then the more likely in this context… A neutral interpretation of the phrase… reads little into the addition of the word \"existence.\" James adds it simply to connote the actual face that a person sees in the mirror: his \"natural\" face… Confirmation… comes from v. 24, where \"his natural face\" is replaced with the simply reflexive pronoun: \"himself.\""
- **locus:** L45–L47
- **passage:** James 1:23

### C-R2-018
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo rejects making the point a contrast in *what* is seen (natural face vs perfect law) or *how carefully* one looks (*katanoeo* vs *parakypto*): *katanoeo* usually means careful contemplation, not a hasty glance; the real contrast is results—forgetting vs continuing, not forgetting, and doing.
- **quote:** "We should probably, then, not find any great significance in James's shift from one verb for \"seeing\" to another in these verses. The point of his analogy lies elsewhere… These results are clearly contrasted with what James says of the person who looks into the perfect law in v. 25… The key failure of the \"hearer only,\" then, is forgetting."
- **locus:** L51–L53
- **passage:** James 1:23–25

### C-R2-019
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo links “forgetting” what one sees in God’s word to the pervasive biblical theme of remembering God’s acts and law (Exod. 13:3; Deut. 6:12; 8:2; Mal. 4:4; 2 Pet. memory theme): remember = contemplate so it imprints heart and mind; forget = superficial reading that does not imprint the soul.
- **quote:** "To \"remember\" God, his acts and his teachings, is to contemplate them in such a way that they make a lasting impression on the heart and the mind. The person who \"forgets\" what he has seen in God's word is one who reads or listens superficially, not imprinting the message on the soul."
- **locus:** L53
- **passage:** James 1:24

### C-R2-020
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo takes the striking shift from “word” (18, 21–23) to “law” (v. 25) as referring not to Mosaic law *as such* but to Mosaic law as interpreted and supplemented by Christ: perfect/eschatological form; “that gives freedom” evokes new-covenant law on the heart with Spirit-enabled obedience (Jer. 31; cf. 1:21); substantially equivalent to the regenerating “word of truth.”
- **quote:** "Taken together, these points suggest that James's \"law\" does not refer to the law of Moses as such, but to the law of Moses as interpreted and supplemented by Christ… Perhaps, then, the addition of the word \"perfect\" connotes the law in its eschatological, \"perfected\" form, while the qualification \"that gives freedom\" refers to the new covenant promise of the law written on the heart… accompanied by a work of the Spirit enabling obedience to that law for the first time."
- **locus:** L57
- **passage:** James 1:25

### C-R2-021
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: the doer “looks intently… continues… not a forgetful hearer but a doer of work” and “will be blessed in what he does”; blessing more likely future salvation from accepting the word (v. 21) than merely present mercy in obedient living—“in his doing” may have causal flavor.
- **quote:** "It is the one who looks intently into the law and perseveres in it who is blessed in what he does… But the blessing is more likely to refer to future blessing - the salvation that comes when one \"accepts\" the word (v. 21). \"In his doing\" may, then, have something of a causal flavor: he will be blessed \"because he has been a doer.\""
- **locus:** L61
- **passage:** James 1:25

### C-R2-022
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo sees 1:26–27 as culmination of accept→do word→do law, giving three manifestations that set the agenda for the rest of the letter: control of tongue (1:19–20; 3:1–12; 4:11–12); concern for the helpless (2:1–13, 15–16; 5:1–6); avoidance of worldliness (4:4–10); true religion in obedient lifestyle is leitmotif of the next four chapters.
- **quote:** "Verses 26-27 culminate this progression, as James suggests three ways in which believers can do the word/law. These three manifestations of obedience to the word introduce or touch on key ideas that James will return to again in the letter… And the idea of these verses - that true religion is manifested in a lifestyle of obedience to God - becomes the leitmotif of the next four chapters. To some extent, then, these verses set the agenda for the rest of the letter."
- **locus:** L63–L69
- **passage:** James 1:26–27

### C-R2-023
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo notes “religious/religion” are rare NT terms for general worship/outward ceremony; James may choose them deliberately for tests of genuine religious experience; failure to rein the tongue = self-deception and “worthless” religion (*mataios*, often of idolatry)—no better than idolatry.
- **quote:** "Perhaps James deliberately chooses such broad terms in order to sharpen his point: anyone who has a claim to genuine religious experience must submit those claims to these tests… Failure to control one's speech, James asserts, means that one is \"deceiving\" oneself about having true religion (see v. 22); that kind of religion is worthless… The \"religion\" that people who do not control their speech have is no better, James suggests, than idolatry."
- **locus:** L71–L73
- **passage:** James 1:26

### C-R2-024
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Citing Calvin, Moo denies that 1:27 defines all true worship: James reminds that religion without these things is nothing; not polemic against ritual per se but against ritual that is only outward show; looking after orphans and widows echoes OT concern (Exod. 22:22; Deut. 14:29; Isa. 1:10–17; Ps. 68:5)—God as “Father”; extends to contemporary helpless.
- **quote:** "As Calvin says, \"[James] does not define generally what religion is, but reminds us that religion without the things he mentions is nothing.\" James is not polemicizing against religious ritual per se but against a ritual that goes no further than outward show and mere words… One test of pure religion, therefore, is the degree to which we extend aid to the \"helpless\" in our world."
- **locus:** L75
- **passage:** James 1:27

### C-R2-025
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo’s third mark of true religion—“keep oneself from being polluted by the world”—guards against reducing pure religion to mere social action; “world” = ungodly worldview/lifestyle of estrangement from the creator; believers must keep “spotless” from the world’s contaminating influence.
- **quote:** "James is careful not to give the impression that religion pleasing to God consists simply in outward acts or in social action. The \"world\" is a common biblical way of referring to the ungodly worldview and lifestyle that characterize human life in its estrangement from the creator. Christians… must constantly work to distance themselves from the way of life that surrounds us on every side - to keep themselves \"spotless\"… from the world's contaminating influence."
- **locus:** L77
- **passage:** James 1:27

### C-R2-026
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo frames James 2:1–13 as application of 1:19–27 to discrimination against the poor in the community: main point is the command of v. 1; three reasons favoritism is evil—(1) contradicts God’s honor of the poor (5–6a); (2) fawning over rich who persecute (6b–7); (3) violates love of neighbor, heart of Jesus’ reinterpretation of the law (8–13).
- **quote:** "The command not to discriminate in v. 1 is therefore the main point of the section… James then gives three specific reasons why favoritism toward the rich and discrimination against the poor are evil. First, such an attitude stands in contradiction to God's own evaluation, who honors the poor (vv. 5-6a). Second, favoritism toward the rich betrays a fawning, servile mentality - for rich people are the very ones who are persecuting the Christian community (vv. 6b-7). And, third, discrimination against the poor violates the demand of love for the neighbor, the centerpiece of Jesus' reinterpretation of the law of God (vv. 8-13)."
- **locus:** L91
- **passage:** James 2:1–13 intro

### C-R2-027
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Between worship-gathering vs. community judicial-assembly scenarios for 2:2–3, Moo slightly prefers weekly worship: “your meeting” points to a definite well-known gathering; main point unaffected either way; v. 6 “you have insulted the poor” implies something like the scenario had occurred, not pure hypothesis.
- **quote:** "On the whole, however, the possessive \"your meeting\" in v. 2 seems to point to a definite, well-known gathering that better fits the worship service than a judicial assembly… He does use language suggesting a hypothetical situation in vv. 2-3; but v. 6 - \"You have insulted the poor\" - implies that something like what James describes here had actually taken place."
- **locus:** L101–L103
- **passage:** James 2:1–4 setting

### C-R2-028
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: lit. “Don’t have faith… with favoritism” makes discriminating inconsistent with true faith in Christ; rejects treating “Lord Jesus Christ” in 2:1 (and 1:1) as interpolation into a purely Jewish document—no textual basis.
- **quote:** "James's way of putting the matter makes clear that discriminating against people is inconsistent with true faith in Christ… a few scholars have thought that both are interpolations into an originally purely Jewish document. But no textual basis exists for the removal of the title, and this view is rightly treated by modern scholars as a curiosity of interpretive history."
- **locus:** L105
- **passage:** James 2:1

### C-R2-029
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** On “our… Lord Jesus Christ” + genitive “glory,” Moo prefers the ambiguous “Lord of glory” style over bare epexegetic title “the glorious one” (glory never alone as title) or simple adjective “glorious Lord”: glory suggests Jesus’ exalted heavenly sphere from which he will save and judge (cf. 5:9)—apt where Christians give too much glory to humans.
- **quote:** "\"Glory\" has enough theological significance in its own right in the NT that turning it into a simple adjective - \"glorious\" - might weaken the sense James intends here… Describing Jesus as the Lord of glory suggests particularly the heavenly sphere to which he has been exalted and from which he will come at the end of history to save and to judge (cf. Jas. 5:9). This reminder is particularly appropriate in a situation where Christians are giving too much \"glory\" to human beings."
- **locus:** L111
- **passage:** James 2:1

### C-R2-030
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: “favoritism” is plural “acts of favoritism,” coined NT rendering of Hebrew partiality—“receiving the face,” judging by external appearance; applies beyond dress to skin color or physical appearance; OT impartiality (Deut. 10:17–18; Lev. 19:15 in same context as love command Lev. 19:18) grounds the ethic.
- **quote:** "To \"receive the face\" means to make judgments about people based on external appearance… the Greek word here is plural - \"acts of favoritism\" (NRSV) - and this makes clear that the prohibition has wide-ranging application. We are not to make decisions about people based on any external factor - whether it be dress, color of skin, or general physical appearance."
- **locus:** L113
- **passage:** James 2:1

### C-R2-031
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo takes *synagoge* as Christian “assembly/meeting” under their control (not ongoing Jewish synagogue attendance only): gold-ringed person in bright/fine clothes vs poor in shabby clothes (same root as 1:21 “filth”); ushers fawn on rich, tell poor to stand or sit by the footstool/floor.
- **quote:** "James's qualification of this \"synagogue\" as \"your synagogue\" implies that Christians had control over the meetings… Into this meeting come two people, distinguished from each other by their dress… In any case, the situation is clear enough: Christians in positions of some authority in the community… are fawning over the rich and treating the poor with disdain and contempt."
- **locus:** L117–L121
- **passage:** James 2:2–3

### C-R2-032
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, double-mindedness, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** For 2:4 *diakrino*, Moo prefers “doubt/waver… in yourselves” over mere “discriminated among yourselves”: links to 1:6 and the letter’s motif of divided heart toward God and others; improper division rich/poor reflects improper divisions in believers’ minds; consistently Christian conduct requires a consistently Christian heart and mind.
- **quote:** "The second interpretation might then be the better option… More importantly, James has already used the verb with just this meaning (1:6) to introduce a key motif in his letter: the warning to Christians not to have a divided heart in their relationship to God and to one another… The improper \"division\" being made between rich and poor reflects the improper \"divisions\" harbored in the minds of the believers. Consistently Christian conduct comes only from a consistently Christian heart and mind."
- **locus:** L123
- **passage:** James 2:4

### C-R2-033
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: discriminators become “judges with evil thoughts”—may echo Lev. 19:15 judicial partiality and/or pejorative claim of God’s judging rights (cf. 4:11–12); “evil thoughts” = evil motives, sinful standards of decision, or verdicts reached.
- **quote:** "When Christians show favoritism toward people in the assembly, they implicitly claim God's own right to stand in judgment over other people. But James's addition of the phrase with evil thoughts leaves no doubt about the negative nature of this \"judging.\""
- **locus:** L125
- **passage:** James 2:4

### C-R2-034
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** First reason favoritism is wrong: it contradicts God’s election—God has chosen the poor (in the world’s eyes) to be rich in faith and inherit the kingdom promised to those who love him (possible echo of Jesus’ beatitude Luke 6:20 / Matt. 5:3); spiritual not material vantage-point should govern Christian evaluation of people.
- **quote:** "First, favoritism toward the rich is wrong because it contradicts God's own attitude, as revealed in his gracious election to salvation… In a stark reversal of status, poor people have become rich in faith… Expanding on the meaning of this spiritual wealth, James adds that they will also inherit the kingdom that he promised to those who love him… It is from this spiritual vantage-point, not the material, that Christians should judge others."
- **locus:** L127–L129
- **passage:** James 2:5

### C-R2-035
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** On *ptochos*, Moo holds material sense is required by 2:2–3, but preferred dative *kosmos* as “in the eyes of the world” (NIV) also allows spiritual nuance (humble dependence); he rejects liberation-theology reading that God chooses *only* the poor—James does not say “only,” and NT (incl. James 1:10–11 as Moo reads it) includes wealthy in the church; yet God delights to grace the discarded, and the church should embody special concern for the poor.
- **quote:** "But to infer from James's positive assertion about poor people a negative verdict on rich people - God does not choose rich people to have faith - is unwarranted… God, the NT suggests, delights especially to shower his grace on those whom the world has discarded and on those who are most keenly aware of their own inadequacy. James calls on the church to embody a similar ethic of special concern for the poor and the helpless."
- **locus:** L131–L141
- **passage:** James 2:5 theology of the poor

### C-R2-036
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Second reason: the rich exploit the (mostly poor) readers, drag them into court, and blaspheme/slander “the noble name… called upon you” (ownership language; probably Christ, light of 2:1)—not counsel against kindness to rich but against undue deference at the poor’s expense; socioeconomic pattern fits first-century Middle East and OT prophetic denunciation (*katadynasteuo*).
- **quote:** "James is not counseling the Christians not to be kind to these rich people; he is simply arguing that they should not give undue deference to them at the expense of the poor… Is it not the rich who are exploiting you?… dragging you into court… slandering the noble name of him to whom you belong… To have a name \"called\" on someone suggests the idea of ownership… Probably James intends either God or, more likely, Christ (in light of v. 1)."
- **locus:** L143–L153
- **passage:** James 2:6–7

### C-R2-037
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Third and most developed argument (2:8–13): partiality is sinful because it violates the love command; 10–11 justify lawbreaker status by law’s indivisibility; 12–13 insist believers will be judged by God’s law—returns to true-religion theme (1:21–27) and anticipates true faith seen in works (2:14–26).
- **quote:** "the attention James devotes to the matter suggests that his third argument against such favoritism is the most important: it violates the law of love (vv. 8-13). The main point comes at the beginning, in vv. 8-9: partiality is sinful because it violates the love command… James insists that believers will have to account for their actions against the standard of God's law. This emphasis on obedience as the criterion in the judgment both returns to the \"true religion\" theme… and anticipates the \"true faith seen in works\" argument of 2:14-26."
- **locus:** L161
- **passage:** James 2:8–13 intro

### C-R2-038
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo prefers *mentoi* as “really/indeed” (context) over “however” (usual NT adversative); “royal law” (*basilikos*, belonging to the king) is not merely the single love command as “supreme,” but the sum of demands God through Jesus imposes—law of the kingdom, OT law as interpreted and handed over in Jesus’ teaching (cf. “perfect law that gives freedom,” 1:25); kata Scripture = completing moral will *in accordance with* love of neighbor.
- **quote:** "\"royal law\" might be James's way of referring to the sum total of demands that God, through Jesus, imposes on believers: \"the whole law as interpreted and handed over to the church in the teaching of Jesus.\"… What James might be suggesting, then, is that completing the sum total of God's will for his people (the moral law) takes place in accordance with conformity to the central demand of that law, love for the neighbor."
- **locus:** L163–L175
- **passage:** James 2:8

### C-R2-039
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo ties royal law/love command to Jesus (Matt. 22:37–40) and early Christian reception (Gal. 5:13–14; Rom. 13:8–10); Jesus expands “neighbor” to all contacts including foreigners and enemies (Luke 10; Matt. 5:44); Leviticus 19 pairs anti-partiality (19:15) with love (19:18), so favoritism violates kingdom law’s heart.
- **quote:** "James is in line with that teaching as he argues that love for the neighbor, the heart of \"the royal law,\" forbids the church from discriminating against any who might enter its doors. And James's application of this love command to the problem of favoritism finds a solid contextual basis in Leviticus 19, where a prohibition of partiality occurs just three verses before the command to love the neighbor."
- **locus:** L179
- **passage:** James 2:8

### C-R2-040
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: show favoritism = “working sin,” convicted by the law as lawbreakers/transgressors; love requires equal respect for shabbily dressed poor and well-dressed, and (extended) welcome across race and status; Christians are to build counterculture living kingdom rather than world values (cf. Gal. 3:28).
- **quote:** "Love for the neighbor, extended by Jesus to all people, including those different from us… requires that poor, shabbily dressed people be given as much respect and attention as the well-dressed and prominent… In obedience to their king, Jesus, Christians are to build among themselves a genuine counterculture, in which the values of the kingdom of God rather than the values of this world are lived out… believers who show favoritism are convicted by the law as lawbreakers."
- **locus:** L181–L183
- **passage:** James 2:9

### C-R2-041
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** On 2:10–11, Moo records Jewish/pagan unity-of-law tradition (4 Macc. 5:20–21; Gal. 5:3; Matt. 5:18–19): stumble at one point = guilty of all (*enochos* judicial guilt); unity rests on one Lawgiver speaking—disobey a commandment is to disobey God; Decalogue adultery/murder (order as in LXX B / Luke 18:20 / Rom. 13:9) illustrate, not necessarily a community literal-murder scenario.
- **quote:** "Critical to the argument is that the commandment is not just a text but 'someone speaking'… the individual commandments are part and parcel of one indivisible whole, because they reflect the will of the one Lawgiver. To violate a commandment is to disobey God himself and render a person guilty before him."
- **locus:** L185–L191
- **passage:** James 2:10–11

### C-R2-042
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo denies that James’s unity argument requires perfect compliance with every ceremonial Mosaic command: unlike Jewish “light vs heavy” examples, James pairs two equal-weight Decalogue commands; applied to “royal law” / “law of liberty” as OT law reinterpreted by Jesus (as Jesus’ Matt. 5:18–19 is tempered by 5:17).
- **quote:** "It is not the OT law per se that he urges perfect compliance with, but \"the royal law\" (v. 8), \"the law of liberty\" (v. 12; cf. 1:25). This \"law\" takes up within it the OT law, but as understood through Jesus' fulfillment of it… so James applies this standard point about the law's unity to the law as reinterpreted by Jesus."
- **locus:** L193
- **passage:** James 2:10–11 scope of law

### C-R2-043
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo on 2:12: continuous speak and act as those about to be judged *by* (instrumental *dia*) the law of liberty—not mere “atmosphere” of law (contra Hort); first explicit eschatological judgment warning; anticipates 2:14–26; law = OT as reinterpreted by Christ; law of liberty = obligation discharged with joy because God liberates from sin’s penalty and enables obedience by the Spirit (implanted word, 1:21).
- **quote:** "For the first time, James warns about eschatological judgment and suggests that conformity to the demands of the law will be the criterion of that judgment… the law in question here is not the OT law as such, but the OT as reinterpreted and imposed by Christ on his followers… For the will of God now confronts us as a law of liberty - an obligation we discharge in the joyful knowledge that God has both \"liberated\" us from the penalty of sin and given us, in his Spirit, the power to obey his will."
- **locus:** L195–L197
- **passage:** James 2:12

### C-R2-044
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: 2:13a proverbial retribution—judgment without mercy for the unmerciful; mercy included in the judging law (Zech. 7:9–10; T. Zebulun 8:1; Jesus’ Matt. 18:21–35 and inverse of Matt. 5:7); mercy is active love, not mere feeling; discrimination is the opposite of mercy.
- **quote:** "So James warns that judgment without mercy will be shown to anyone who has not been merciful… Being \"merciful,\" as these texts suggest, is not merely a feeling of concern, but involves actively reaching out to show love to others. The discrimination that James's readers are practicing is the opposite of such mercy; and if they continue on this path, they will find at the end of their lives a judgment \"without mercy.\""
- **locus:** L201
- **passage:** James 2:13a

### C-R2-045
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** On “Mercy triumphs over judgment,” Moo prefers human mercy (context of v. 12/13a) over primarily God’s mercy: merciful attitude/actions evidence desire to obey kingdom law and a heart made right by grace; the believer never perfectly keeps royal law (vv. 10–11) but mercy evidences union with Christ who fulfilled the law—basis of confidence of vindication at judgment.
- **quote:** "But the \"mercy\" that James has been referring to in this context is human mercy, not God's (v. 12). We therefore think it more likely that he is making a point about the way in which the mercy we show toward others shows our desire to obey the law of the kingdom and, indirectly therefore, of a heart made right by the work of God's grace… our merciful attitude and actions will count as evidence of the presence of Christ within us. And it is on the basis of this union with the one who perfectly fulfilled the law for us that we can have confidence of vindication at the judgment."
- **locus:** L203
- **passage:** James 2:13b
